vocabulary.definition: The twisted-ladder molecule that stores the instructions for building and running a living thing.
The twisted-ladder shape of a DNA molecule — two strands wound around each other.
Two matching letters (A-T or C-G) that sit across from each other and form a rung of the DNA ladder.
The enzyme that unwinds and unzips the DNA double helix into two single strands.
The enzyme that builds a new DNA strand by reading a template strand and adding matching bases to it.
An original DNA strand that gets used as the pattern for building a new matching strand.
The way DNA copies itself so every new molecule keeps one old strand and gains one new strand.
A copying mistake in the DNA sequence that can change how a gene works.

structureCards.label: Helix Unwinds
structureCards.definition: The stage where the two intact strands of the DNA double helix begin to come apart, starting the copying process.
structureCards.function: Helicase, an enzyme, breaks the hydrogen bonds holding each base pair together and unwinds the twisted double helix at this point, like unzipping a spiral zipper.
structureCards.whereItIs: At the top of the model (y ≈ +6.5), where the still-twisted double helix meets the replication fork and the two backbones begin to splay apart.
structureCards.whyItMatters: Nothing else in replication can happen until the helix is unwound — the bases have to be exposed before any new strand can be built alongside them.

structureCards.label: Strands Separate
structureCards.definition: The stage where the two backbone strands, now unwound, pull fully apart into a Y-shaped replication fork, exposing their unpaired bases.
structureCards.function: Once helicase has broken the base-pair bonds, the two single strands physically separate and curve outward, each becoming an independent template strand with its row of bases exposed.
structureCards.whereItIs: Middle-upper segment of the model (y ≈ +2), at the vertex of the Y where the two backbones diverge.
structureCards.whyItMatters: Each separated strand is what the copying machinery actually reads — without full separation, DNA polymerase would have nothing exposed to match new bases against.

structureCards.label: New Strands Built
structureCards.definition: The stage where a brand-new, complementary strand is constructed alongside each of the two original template strands.
structureCards.function: DNA polymerase reads each template strand and matches free-floating nucleotides to it using base-pairing rules (A with T, G with C), building a new strand base by base.
structureCards.whereItIs: Middle-lower segment of the model (y ≈ -2), between the two forming daughter strands where new base-pair rungs are actively reappearing.
structureCards.whyItMatters: This is the actual copying step — it's where the genetic information from the original strand gets physically duplicated into a second, matching strand.

structureCards.label: Two DNA Copies Formed
structureCards.definition: The finished result: two complete double helices, each built from one original strand and one newly built strand.
structureCards.function: The two new strand-pairs re-twist into full double helices, producing two DNA molecules that are structurally identical to the starting molecule.
structureCards.whereItIs: Bottom segment of the model (y ≈ -6.5), where the two fully re-formed double helices sit side by side.
structureCards.whyItMatters: This is why replication exists: a dividing cell needs two complete, accurate copies of its DNA so each daughter cell inherits a full instruction set.
